articles.title: H.264 Is Magic (2016)
articles.summary: H.264 is a video compression codec standard that has revolutionized the way we transmit and store video content. By throwing away less important bits, H.264 is able to compress video files to a tiny fraction of their original size, making it possible to store large amounts of data on small devices. This is achieved through a complex algorithm that analyzes the video frame and identifies the most important pixels to keep. The result is a 3D array of bytes that can be stored in a relatively small amount of space. This technology has far-reaching implications for the development of devices such as smartphones, drones, and security cameras, which all rely on H.264 compression to transmit and store video content.

articles.title: Extremely brief history of PDP computers
articles.summary: The PDP-11 family of minicomputers has a fascinating history that spans over four decades, with significant advancements in technology and market demand. The pdp-1 was an experiment in the early 1970s, but it wasn't called a computer at the time due to its similarity to industrial control systems. The pdp-4 was a variant of the pdp-1 that was slower and more expensive, but it was eventually upgraded to become the pdp-7. This was followed by the pdp-5, which was created to be smaller and cheaper for industrial control systems, but was still intended for the same market. The pdp-6 was a different beast, aimed at a different market, and supported directly-addressable memory and memory protection. The pdp-10 was a powerful machine that ran Lisp well, but was eventually replaced by the VAX, which eventually subsumed the pdp-10.

articles.title: Apple's git still trusts the compromised eMudhra certificates
articles.summary: Apple's git still trusts the compromised eMudhra certificates, which means that even though the certificates have been compromised, the developer tools that ship with macOS, including git, curl and python3, still use them to authenticate connections to GitHub and other HTTPS servers. This can leave developers vulnerable to interception and tampering of their credentials and data. The compromised certificates can be used to impersonate GitHub and steal credentials, and anyone on the network path between the developer and GitHub can intercept traffic. To check whether a git is affected, developers can run the command git ls-remote https://git-emudra.we-have-a-problem.com/check.git, which will display a certificate error if the git is compromised. To prevent this, developers can remove the affected roots from /etc/ssl/cert.pem, which can be done manually, and repeat the checks after every update until Apple ships a fix.
